offence_severity: Death sentence (minimum/maximum not specified, but life imprisonment awarded with 35 years minimum)
physical_harm: Grievous injuries resulting in death by asphyxia caused by strangulation
number_of_offences: Charged under Sections 302, 376, and 450 IPC; death sentence upheld for Section 302, life imprisonment for Sections 376 and 450
premeditation_planning: Court found premeditation/planning as the crime was committed in a premeditated manner
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the DNA report showing the presence of the appellant's semen in the vaginal swab of the deceased and the finding that she died of asphyxia caused by strangulation.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the child witness (PW-2) as credible because he understood the questions put to him and was able to answer them, and there was no evidence that he was tutored.

legal_representation.state: Mishra Saurabh, Vanshaja Shukla, Ankit Lal

appeal_history.supreme_court: Set aside death sentence, awarded life imprisonment

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant, aged 32 years, was asked by the father of the victim-deceased to stay at his house with his four children on the fateful night. The appellant consumed liquor, asked the deceased aged 14 years to sleep elsewhere, and then committed rape on her, causing grievous injuries resulting in her death. The incident was witnessed by the brother of the deceased, who narrated the incident to his parents in the morning. The case was registered under Sections 302, 376, and 450 IPC. The trial court convicted the appellant and awarded death sentence, which was affirmed by the High Court.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant had been falsely implicated by the family of the deceased at the instance of the police. They contended that there was no eye-witness in the case and that the child witness, Sanchit Jojo, could not be relied upon because he did not raise any alarm after the incident and did not inform his parents about the incident in the morning. The defence also claimed that the prosecution could not furnish explanation on various counts and that the facts and circumstances of the case did not warrant the death sentence as awarded by the courts below.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the extreme penalty of death need not be inflicted except in gravest cases of extreme culpability. It emphasized that life imprisonment is the rule and death sentence is an exception, and that the court must consider both the circumstances of the offender and the crime before awarding the death penalty.
precedent_relied_upon: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Ramesh & Anr., (2011) 4 SCC 786; Suryanarayana v. State of Karnataka, AIR 2001 SC 482; Ramnaresh & Ors. v. State of Chhattisgarh, AIR 2012 SC 1357; Munish Mubar v. State of Haryana, AIR 2013 SC 912; Raj Kumar Singh alias Raju @ Batya v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 2013 SC 3150; Prithipal Singh & Ors. v. State of Punjab & Anr., (2012) 1 SCC 10; Neel Kumar alias Anil Kumar v. State of Haryana, (2012) 5 SCC 766; Gian Chand & Ors. v. State of Haryana, AIR 2013 SC 3395; Prajeet Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar, (2008) 4 SCC 434; Kamta Tiwari v. State of M.P., AIR 1996 SC 2800; Dhananjoy Chatterjee @ Dhana v. State of W.B., (1994) 2 SCC 220; Bantu @ Naresh Giri v. State of M.P., AIR 2002 SC 70; Mohinder Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 2013 SC 3622; Swami Shraddananda @ Murali Manohar Mishra v. State of Karnataka, AIR 2008 SC 3040
sentencing_rationale: The Supreme Court held that although the appellant had committed a heinous crime and raped an innocent, helpless, and defenceless minor girl who was in his custody, it was not a case which falls within the category of 'rarest of rare' cases. Therefore, the death sentence was set aside and life imprisonment was awarded.
other_sentence_order: The appellant must serve a minimum of 35 years in jail without remission, before consideration of his case for pre-mature release. However, it would be subject to clemency power of the Executive.
